Q: How to join the tables in codeigniter? A:

CodeIgniter has a dedicated query builder method to render a SUM() expression in the SELECT clause. It will apply identifier quoting to its first parameter if no single quote or parenthesis is found in the text. To ensure a valid expression wrap the condition in otherwise useless parentheses.

When JOINing on identical column names, pass only the column name as the second parameter of join(). This will render a valid USING() expression. In this case, using USING also disambiguates the GROUP BY column.

return $this->db
    ->select('bi.*')
    ->select_sum('(uv.user_action = 1)', 'likes')
    ->select_sum('(uv.user_action = 2)', 'dislikes')
    ->join('user_votes', 'idea_id')
    ->group_by('idea_id')
    ->get('business_ideas bi')
    ->result();

Q: How does provenance work in a kernel in Rust? A:

In the current version of Rust's abstract machine, the global allocator is a special case. I believe this to be a mistake, and am considering proposing a Rust RFC to change this. But here's how things currently work:

  • If you obtain memory from the global allocator, it will come with provenance already attached to it, and you must use that provenance in order to access that memory. If you free that memory, and later allocate memory that happens to be at the same address, it is effectively new memory (and will arrive with a different provenance, so you won't be able to access it using an old pointer that happens to share an address).

  • For statically allocated memory (memory that is allocated on program startup, such as the memory used to store static variables, or the memory pointed to by references to constants like &0 or string literals), you will typically only be able to access it via shared references. (For backwards compatibility, unsafe code can create an &mut to a static mut variable, but it is usually better to use Sync wrappers around UnsafeCell instead nowadays.) Such references will always come with an appropriate provenance to access that statically allocated memory, and you must use that provenance to access it. Because &'static references never become invalid, it isn't observable whether shared references to the same memory obtained this way share a provenance or not – they will all be valid in any case.

  • A function/method will be given memory in which to store its parameters and local variables. If for some reason you want to form a raw pointer to them, you can use &raw const/&raw mut to get a suitable provenance.

  • Those are the only three ways to obtain memory in stable, safe Rust. But with unsafe Rust, you can obtain memory in other ways (e.g. by obtaining it from the operating system via FFI or inline assembly, or (if you are the operating system) by reconfiguring the page tables). I believe the intention behind the rules for this to be:

    • If such memory was obtained directly using assembly code, and is not currently considered "part of the Rust abstract machine", you can create a pointer to it using from_exposed_provenance. On most platforms, assuming the program itself is allowed to access the memory, that resulting pointer will have a valid provenance for that memory.1 From then on, you can use that provenance that you obtained from from_exposed_provenance to manipulate the memory. If you later use from_exposed_provenance to recreate another pointer to the same memory, you will get the same pointer with the same provenance again.1

      One subtlety here is that doing anything with the original pointer (or a recreated version of it) will invalidate any references derived from it (except that reading through it won't invalidate shared references derived from it). As such, the correct way to use this sort of memory is that whenever you convert memory obtained via such a pointer into a reference, you should access the memory only via that reference until the reference's lifetime ends, and must also ensure that that memory remains valid until the reference's lifetime ends. (Normally if you are doing something allocator-like, you would use a raw pointer to return the allocation to the Box or other allocator-tracking class, and let it convert the pointer into a reference – Box and friends know how to manage the reference lifetimes correctly, and this will save you the trouble of needing to do it yourself.)

      Note that a reference that's derived from a pointer won't necessarily have the same provenance as the pointer itself – if the pointer's provenance was valid to access the memory, the reference's will be too, but subsequent accesses via the reference's provenance won't invalidate the reference whereas subsequent accesses via the pointer's provenance will. (This is the current rule – there have been discussions about relaxing it, but it is not going to become stronger, so complying with it will be sufficient.)

    • If such memory was obtained from C code, you should assume that its provenance was created according to C's provenance rules (due to the possibility of cross-language optimization). The last time I looked, C's provenance rules weren't really nailed down yet, but the C language committee seemed to be leaning in the direction of treating an integer-to-pointer cast as equivalent to Rust's from_exposed_provenance and compilers are likely implementing it like that too. So the provenance would work as in the previous section, unless something C-specific had happened to limit the provenance:

      • If the memory has gone via a *restrict pointer at the C level, you can't access the memory except via that pointer or pointers derived from it, for as long as that pointer is in scope (basically the same rule as for Rust &mut).
      • The type of pointer via which the value is passed from C to Rust is considered (by the C compiler) to be the type at which Rust is performing the accesses, so the same memory can't simultaneously be accessed at a different type unless one of C's exceptions applies. Luckily, one of the exceptions is that using a pointer of character type is always legal for this, so a simple way to avoid breaking the rule is to pass the C pointer as (from C's point of view) an unsigned char *, at which point nothing Rust does can violate this specific rule of C.

The remaining case is "if I implement the global allocator myself, how is the provenance handled for that?". I don't think the rules for this have been nailed down yet – I personally believe that the correct rule is "pretend that the allocations are mutable references that borrow from the memory you provide and ensure that you handle provenance in a way that's compatible with that", and that following this rule would be sufficient to ensure that you don't run into provenance-related trouble, but I don't think that that's actually documented anywhere. (If this rule does work, you would be able to later repurpose heap memory as userspace or device-mapped memory and vice versa, as long as you ensure that no references to it or allocations from it remain at the time you repurpose it.) One word of caution: Rust's optimizer backend LLVM contains a number of global-allocator-specific optimizations that rely on it actually behaving like a global allocator (in particular, LLVM assumes that it's safe to optimize out an allocate+deallocate combination if it doesn't need as much heap memory as the program suggests it does, so the allocation requests implied by the program might not all be visible to the global allocator).

The special cases are specifically for the global allocator, and other allocators do not have them. (That said, the rules for non-global allocators in Rust are not only explicitly subject to change, they almost certainly will change in the future because there are a number of design issues with them. So if you're relying on unstable code to use non-global allocators, you can probably expect to have to change this in the future.)

In any case, kernels have a bit of a problem when they're dealing with pointers taken from userspace ABIs: normally you would want the userspace to give you a pointer it had provenance over, but userspace sometimes isn't so cooperative and might give you a wild or dangling pointer (it is not in general sound for a kernel to assume that the userspace programs it is running will obey memory safety rules). On platforms that don't track provenance at the hardware level, the basic way to deal with this in a kernel is to ensure that, while memory is accessible to userspace, the kernel never forms references to it and accesses it only via raw pointers (and, of course, to check that any pointer you receive from userspace is actually in the range that the process providing it is allowed to access!). This is compatible with all the rules above: you can ignore any provenance you receive from userspace and just pass its address through from_exposed_provenance in order to get a valid pointer (because once you have verified that the userspace was allowed to access the memory and thus that there are no in-kernel references to it, this will recreate a valid pointer to the memory in question). Most processors aren't able to transmit provenances through kernel ABIs anyway, so the usual way to handle this would be to document the type as a pointer from the userspace point of view, but actually treat it as a usize on the kernel side of the interface (if you're on a platform where the two have the same representation, as is usually the case).

If the platform does track provenance at the hardware level, you will need to check the provenance provided by userspace manually – if you try to use the provenance provided by userspace directly the kernel will crash if userspace provided a bad pointer, and if you try to use a kernel-provided provenance then userspace would be able to bypass the hardware checking by tricking the kernel into accessing memory for it that it couldn't access itself, so there is no option other than replicating the hardware's checks yourself.

1 A few platforms track an approximation of provenance at the hardware level, in which case the situation is more complicated and you will need to do something platform-specific to ensure that the provenance matches at the hardware level too. I think the only such platform currently available to consumers is ARM MTE, on which you would need to use hardware instructions to generate a new "tag" (provenance) and tell the hardware that that tag was the tag that was allowed to access the memory, and to arithmetically encode that tag into the pointer you were using. From Rust's point of view, pointers with different hardware provenances have different addresses (because ARM MTE encodes the provenance into bits that Rust sees as part of the pointer address), so from_exposed_provenance would continue to work as on other platforms: same address means same exposed provenance. CHERI is a platform currently under development that also requires hardware instructions to access the provenance, but it is able to return a pointer-with-provenance directly from assembly code and thus you wouldn't need to go via an address at all.

Q: QBWC error QBWC1013: "Could not start QuickBooks." A:

If you move the Quickbooks Company File on your computer, or to a different computer, QB Web Connector's link with QB Time (formerly TSheets) will break.

There is a dedicated button on the Quickbooks integration on QB Time. Click this and then reconnect the sync.

Q: Prevent sleep mode python (Wakelock on python) A:

While googling around to find a solution there was no package available, so I decided to package it to put it to PyPI: wakepy. I got PRs for cross-platform support, and currently wakepy supports Windows, Linux and macOS.

CLI

python -m wakepy [-p]

Using the optional -p flag will use a presentation mode, which keeps the screen on & unlocked.

Python API

Prevent sleep:

from wakepy import keep

with keep.running():
    # do stuff that takes long time

Prevent screensaver/screen lock (and sleep):

from wakepy import keep

with keep.presenting():
    # do stuff that takes long time
